kind_note: Not a repair campaign and not a soak. No gen_configs.py grid, no run_experiments.py, no ideal comparison and no scoring columns; the CSVs are one row per run of compare_engines.py, carrying resource and profile-counter columns. It shares its row schema with 2026-08-03-libspot-soak, whose soak.py it drives, and nothing in it is comparable with the repair campaigns. merge_experiments.py does not read it.
question: What running SPOT simplification inside counter buys over spawning ltlfilt for it, in wall time, in memory, and in whether the answer changes. The 2026-08-03 soak could not answer this: both of its arms were in-process and varied only the deadline tier, so it priced no boundary at all. This campaign runs the same example, seed and shape under simplify_engine = "libspot" and = "ltlfilt" and reads the difference.
decision: In-process simplification was not merged. It buys 4.3% of campaign wall time and no extra completions, against a peak resident set of 24.99 GB inside counter's own address space where the subprocess arm never exceeded 0.18 GB. feat/profiling-harness stays unmerged and is held by provenance/libspot-soak; the cost it targeted is instead being attacked from the subprocess side by the ltlfilt batcher (pull request #65), which keeps the work in a child.

profile_commit.subject: feat(scripts): add a 24-hour soak harness for the in-process libspot paths

profile_commit_evidence: Both hosts' counter-soak worktrees were at this commit for the whole run and still were when the results were pulled down on 2026-08-05 (`git rev-parse HEAD` on each). It is the same commit the soak ran at, deliberately: reusing the soak's pinned binary is what makes the two campaigns' resource figures comparable. Note that it does not contain the driver -- see vendored_scripts.compare_engines.py.
binary_commit_note: Recorded, not inferred: `counter --version` was captured into each host's manifest.json at startup and reads commit=81a46a9, dirty=0 on both. The binary is the one the soak used, never rebuilt for this campaign. It contains both engines; the arms differ in the simplify_engine configuration key and in nothing else. The commit is not an ancestor of main and will not become one, so provenance/libspot-soak is what holds it. Never delete that tag.

run_window.note: UTC, taken from the started_at column of the first and last row, so the end is the start of the final run rather than its finish. Both hosts printed `compare finished` and exited on their own. av3's historical clock skew (~17 min fast) is not corrected for and does not matter: every comparison is between two runs on the same host, and no figure here is derived from a timestamp.

libspot.note: Simplification runs inline in counter under the process-wide libspot lock, falling back to a spawn when the lock is not free inside its 8 ms budget.

ltlfilt.note: Simplification spawns ltlfilt per call. This is the arm that matches main, which has no in-process path at all.

arms.pairing: Engines alternate inside a seed rather than running one arm to completion, so a machine that drifts drifts across both arms instead of under one of them. Seeds are split across hosts and engines never are, so every comparison is within-host and within-seed.
arms.shape: 26 examples x 4 seeds x 2 engines per host = 208 runs each, 416 total. generations = 10, population_size = 300, 300 s wall cap, parallel = 8. Both ltl2tgba_timeout_ms and simplify_timeout_ms are 0, so no deadline fires and no work moves to a detached worker: the engine key is the whole of what separates the arms.

code_under_test: src/runner/spot_inprocess.cpp on feat/profiling-harness -- simplification through libspot behind one process-wide timed_mutex -- against src/runner/ltlfilt.cpp's one_shot_simplify, which spawns the tool. The translation path (run_ltl2tgba_for_counting) has no engine key and is in process in BOTH arms, which is the first caveat below.

results.correctness: 174 of 174 uncapped pairs agree by digest. The in-process simplifier does not change the answer. 13 of those pairs agree on the empty digest, having found nothing in either arm; they are counted in the 174 because a matched empty result is still a match, but they carry no signal.
results.wall: Median ratio ltlfilt/libspot 1.457 over the 174 uncapped pairs longer than 0.5 s (p10 1.178, p90 1.741). Totalled over those pairs the in-process arm saves 19.1%. Totalled over ALL 208 pairs it saves 4.3%, and 4.3% is the figure that describes a campaign: 34 pairs hit the 300 s cap, in-process cannot shorten a run that never finishes, and the capped runs dominate the total.
results.completion: Identical. 174 of 208 within the cap in each arm. In-process buys no completions it did not already have.
results.resources: Peak resident set of THE COUNTER PROCESS ITSELF per run, over all 208 pairs -- see the caveat on sampler scope: libspot median 0.07 GB, p90 0.63, p99 6.20, max 24.99; ltlfilt 0.05 / 0.06 / 0.09 / 0.18. In 59 of 208 pairs libspot held over twice ltlfilt's peak. The extremes are a capped humanoid-531 at 24.99 GB against 0.08, and a detector run that COMPLETED NORMALLY in both arms at 13.18 GB against 0.05. This measures WHERE the memory sits, not how much the machine used: in the ltlfilt arm the same simplification work is happening inside children the sampler never looked at. That is the point rather than a flaw -- memory in a child is bounded by exec, reclaimed on exit and killable on its own, and memory in counter is none of those -- but the pair of figures is not a machine-level total and must not be read as one. There is no setrlimit anywhere on either path, so nothing bounds either side by bytes; the only limits are wall-clock and concurrency.
results.boundary: 231,861 simplify calls in the libspot arm, of which 53,632 (23.1%) found the lock busy inside the 8 ms budget and spawned anyway. The arm is not exec-free: 266,601 fork+exec calls against the ltlfilt arm's 469,184. The 4.3% is therefore the ACHIEVED saving at parallel = 8, not the saving a free lock would give, and the lock's share of lost benefit grows with parallel.

caveats: This prices simplification alone. Translation has no engine key -- run_ltl2tgba_for_counting is in process in both arms -- so about 85% of libspot calls are covered and the rest are not. The direction matters: a full revert to out-of-process removes memory this comparison never charged to the in-process arm, so the resource gap above is a lower bound on what reverting recovers, and the 4.3% is an upper bound on what reverting costs.

The sampler watches counter and nothing else. soak.py reads VmRSS from /proc/<counter pid>/status, so every peak_rss_kb here excludes every tool child. Nothing in this campaign measured how large ltl2tgba, ltlsynt, black or ganak actually grow, and these CSVs cannot be used to size a per-tool memory limit -- that needs a sampler walking the process tree, which none of this work has. What the column does establish is the location of the memory, which is what the arms differ in.

Every peak_rss_kb is a lower bound from second-resolution polling. Both hosts ran soak.py at blob f5a725f5, the 1.0 s sampler; the 0.25 s revision (ab2fe16) was committed but never reached them, exactly as in the soak. The bound understates both arms, so the comparison holds and the absolute peaks do not -- the true libspot maximum is above 24.99 GB, not below it.

Pairs where either side hit the 300 s wall cap are excluded from the correctness and wall-ratio figures, 34 of 208. A capped run dies on SIGKILL, skips the atexit profile report, writes no repairs and hashes to the empty digest e3b0c44298fc1c14; comparing two of those measures the cap. They are kept in the resource figures, where the peak is real however the run ended -- which is why six of the eight runs above 2 GB are capped ones.

av2 carried two stray strace processes at ~52% CPU each (running since ~2026-07-29, unrelated to this work) and two btop instances; av3 was idle. No cross-host wall comparison is drawn, and the pairing makes none necessary.

n = 4 seeds per host. The campaign was cut from 10 seeds on one host to 4 on each of two after the first sizing put it at 9-11 wall hours against a 09:00 deadline. It is powered to separate a 1.46x median from 1.0 and is not powered to resolve small per-example differences.

The corpus keeps its expensive examples rather than trimming them. full-arbiter, humanoid-531, prioritized-arbiter and amba average 167-178 s and cap 45-54% of the time, and they carry the completion-rate signal -- which is the effect most worth catching, and the one that came back identical.

vendored_scripts.note: Verbatim copies of what ran, so the directory reproduces without the git history. Verify a copy with `git hash-object <file>`. compare_engines.py is the unusual one: it was never committed anywhere, so this archive is the first and only commit of that blob rather than a copy of one held elsewhere.

compare_engines.py.basis: recorded: written on 2026-08-04 in the feat/profiling-harness worktree and staged to both hosts, where it stayed untracked (`git status` reports it as `??` on both) and still hashes to this blob. It exists in no commit on that branch, so unlike the soak's drivers it is NOT held by provenance/libspot-soak; committing this copy is what gives the blob a reachable home. Do not refresh it against any later revision -- there is nothing to refresh it from.

soak.py.basis: recorded: compare_engines.py imports soak and calls soak.run_one, so this is the module that actually executed every run. Both hosts' copies hash to this blob, checked on 2026-08-05 after the campaign closed. Same blob the soak archive vendors, and the same 1.0 s sampler revision -- see the second caveat.

analyse_engines.py.basis: recorded: written on 2026-08-05 to read this campaign, and landing at scripts/analyse_engines.py in the same commit that adds this directory, so the vendored copy and the maintained one start identical. Every figure under results was produced by it, from the CSVs in this directory.
